en.title: Investor Pitches Pokémon Apocalypse: Cards as Currency in a Ruined World
en.summary: An accidental pitch from a gaming investor has sparked imagination: a post-apocalyptic world where Pokémon cards become the ultimate currency. It's a wild concept that taps into the enduring, almost unbelievable, value of the franchise.
en.body:
What happens when the world ends? For **Peter Levin**, co-founder of Griffin Gaming Partners, the answer might involve a surprising amount of pocket monsters. In a recent discussion, Levin mused about a hypothetical apocalypse, suggesting that **Pokémon cards** would immediately become the global currency. It’s a bold statement, but one rooted in the franchise’s undeniable, decades-long global appeal and its astonishing performance in the collectibles market, even outperforming major stock indices.

> "Pokemon is a global phenomenon... I'm absolutely convinced that if the world suffered an apocalypse tomorrow, the following day the global currency would be Pokemon cards. Pokemon cards are beating the S&P 500 by 3,000%."

This idea, though born from a hypothetical, has resonated because it taps into the very real, sometimes extreme, value placed on rare Pokémon collectibles. We've seen reports of Japanese organized crime using cards for illicit activities and audacious store robberies across the US, all testament to the astronomical sums some rare cards command. However, the inherent value of these cards, outside of the passionate fan base, is intrinsically tied to the real-world economy. Without dedicated buyers and the continuous flow of currency, their worth would indeed be reduced to mere paper.

## A Fan-Made Pokémon Apocalypse Emerges

While Levin's apocalyptic currency theory is purely speculative, the concept of a **Pokémon**-themed post-apocalypse is already being explored by dedicated fans. A fan-made project, reportedly built using **RPG Maker** and slated for a 2026 release, envisions a grim future where Pokémon are not companions, but resources to be sacrificed in a ruined world. This darker take, distinct from the lighter, companion-focused narratives often seen in the franchise like in **Pokemon the Movie: Everyone's Story**, flips the script entirely. It prompts a fascinating question for fans: what would a world without the established order, but still with Pokémon, truly look like? The idea of surviving with these creatures, even in a brutal, resource-scarce environment, offers a compelling narrative space.

## The Enduring Appeal of Endings

The fascination with post-apocalyptic settings is a well-established phenomenon in gaming and media, with titles like **Fallout**, **The Last of Us**, and **Horizon Zero Dawn** offering iconic visions of humanity's end. The appeal often lies in exploring human resilience, societal collapse, and the moral compromises made in the face of extinction. Introducing Pokémon into this established genre creates a unique juxtaposition. It forces a re-evaluation of what these creatures represent – from beloved companions to potential survival tools or even dangerous remnants of a lost era. The fan-made RPG Maker project, by focusing on the sacrifice of Pokémon, directly confronts this darker potential, offering a stark contrast to the franchise's usual optimistic outlook.

## What's Next for the Apocalypse?

While Levin's pitch remains a thought experiment, the fan-made Pokémon apocalypse game is reportedly targeting a 2026 release. Further details on its development and potential platforms have not yet been announced. As for the franchise itself, its continued dominance in the collectibles and gaming spheres suggests that even in hypothetical doomsday scenarios, Pikachu and friends might just be the last ones standing.

content_raw: For more than three decades, Pokemon and its various card and video games have enjoyed sustained popularity around the world. And at least one prominent collector and investor--Griffin Gaming Partners co-founder Peter Levin--believes that Pokemon's enduring appeal not only extends to the present, it could continue even if the world suddenly came to an end. "Pokemon is a global phenomenon," Levin told The Hollywood Reporter . "I'm absolutely convinced that if the world suffered an apocalypse tomorrow, the following day the global currency would be Pokemon cards. Pokemon cards are beating the S&P 500 by 3,000%. Emanating from Japan, it really took hold around the world in the late '90s and early 2000s. It then had a zenith moment and then a nadir moment, and ever since then, it's been on a parabolic growth curve." As unlikely as that scenario might seem, there could be a very entertaining movie based on survivors using Pokemon cards as currency during an apocalypse. It would be probably even better with actual Pokemon--like the Detective Pikachu movie--but Levin's really hit on fun idea even if it doesn't have a basis in reality. Everything Levin said about Pokemon's popularity is correct. There's a reason why the Japanese mob reportedly used rare Pokemon cards to launder money or for increasingly brazen robberies of Pokemon cards from stores across the US. Some people are willing to pay ridiculous amounts of money for the rarest Pokemon cards and collectibles. However, that value can only hold if the cards have some intrinsic value outside of Pokemon fans. They're only valuable as long as someone puts real currency toward them. Without that network of dedicated buyers, Pokemon cards wouldn't be worth the paper they're printed on when the world goes to hell. Before any potential apocalypse comes along, Pokemon is getting a new stop-motion animated series on Disney+. The September 2026 events for Pokemon Go were also recently announced. Earlier this summer, Pokemon Pokopia received a DLC update as well.
